title: Airplane!
director: Jim Abrahams, David Zucker, Jerry Zucker
logline: Disaster-movie parody aboard a doomed flight. Rapid-fire puns, literalism and sight gags.
overview: An ex-fighter pilot is forced to take over the controls of an airliner when the flight crew succumbs to food poisoning.
tagline: What's slower than a speeding bullet, and able to hit tall buildings at a single bound?

jokes.text: Intercom announcements about the white zone and red zone repeat and contradict each other, then escalate into a marital argument between the two PA voices
jokes.setup: An airport PA system makes routine announcements about the white zone and red zone for passenger loading/unloading — mundane, bureaucratic, ignored by everyone
jokes.punchline: The two anonymous PA voices begin arguing with each other, the abstractions of 'white zone' and 'red zone' become a proxy for a bitter domestic argument, culminating in 'Listen, Betty, don't start up with your white zone shit again'
jokes.explanation: One of Airplane!'s signature opening gambits. The joke works on multiple levels: it subverts the total anonymity and boredom of airport PA announcements by revealing a fully-formed dysfunctional marriage hiding behind the institutional voice. The escalation is perfectly paced — it goes from procedural repetition to ambiguity to open domestic hostility with 'white zone shit,' a phrase whose absurdity is maximized by how straight it's delivered. The gradual reveal structure is masterful: the audience doesn't even realize it's a joke for several beats, making the payoff land harder. Comfortably in 8+ territory.

jokes.text: Hare Krishna solicitor offers flower; passenger responds 'No, thanks. We gave at the office.'
jokes.setup: A Hare Krishna solicitor approaches passengers asking for donations, a familiar annoyance of 1970s-80s airports
jokes.punchline: The passenger brushes off a religious donation request with 'We gave at the office' — the standard deflection for charity solicitations, applied absurdly to a spiritual/religious ask
jokes.explanation: Clean little joke — the mundane corporate-charity deflection applied to spiritual giving is a compact absurdist swap. Economy is excellent (four words for the punchline). Not particularly original but well-structured and gets a solid laugh.

jokes.text: PA voices' argument about the zones transitions into the topic of abortion: 'You want me to have an abortion.'
jokes.setup: The white zone/red zone argument has been building; audience expects more zone bickering
jokes.punchline: The argument abruptly escalates to: 'You want me to have an abortion. It's the only sensible thing to do.'
jokes.explanation: This is the callback payoff to the PA argument — the logical, insane endpoint of a marital spat that began as airport bureaucracy. The jump from zone logistics to abortion is a spectacular escalation that makes the joke exponentially funnier than its setup. The deadpan institutional delivery of 'it's the only sensible thing to do' over a public address system makes it transgressive and hilarious. Earns its 8+ score because the buildup, structure, and shock of escalation are all expertly calibrated.

jokes.text: Hare Krishna solicitor approaches another passenger; the solicitor is apparently assaulted off-screen mid-approach — implying violent audience frustration with airport solicitors
jokes.setup: The Hare Krishna solicitor approaches yet another passenger with his flower pitch, beginning 'Would you care...'
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts off abruptly at '03:52' mid-sentence — implying (from context and the film's visual gags) that the solicitor has been violently dispatched. The running gag of the solicitor being progressively neutralized pays off here.
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff — each time the solicitor appears, something worse happens to him, escalating the dark comedy of airport-solicitor frustration to its logical violent extreme. The cutaway (not showing the violence) is good technique. Solid running-gag execution.

jokes.text: Baggage handler asks where the forklift is; it's found — then 'Look out!' followed by implied chaos (a person gets scooped/injured by the forklift)
jokes.setup: Two baggage handlers casually ask about a forklift's location, completely routine
jokes.punchline: 'Look out!' — something (or someone) has clearly been impaled or scooped by the forklift in an escalating slapstick gag, cutting away before we see the full carnage
jokes.explanation: Classic Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker background slapstick — something horrible happening with no narrative consequence while the main characters are occupied elsewhere. The cutaway structure is key: we hear 'Look out!' and can only imagine. Functional physical comedy, not especially sophisticated but well-timed.

jokes.text: Ted watches Elaine leave dramatically; a passerby glances at the scene and says flatly: 'What a pisser.'
jokes.setup: Ted and Elaine have a heartfelt, melodramatic romantic breakup scene with intense emotional dialogue
jokes.punchline: A completely uninvolved bystander summarizes the entire emotional scene with the deflating, profane understatement: 'What a pisser.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan punctuation of an overwrought dramatic scene. The ZAZ technique of using an oblivious bystander to deflate melodrama with brutally casual language is efficiently executed here. 'What a pisser' is exactly three words, profane but mild, and utterly insufficient for the drama it's responding to — that gap IS the joke. Strong economy score.

jokes.text: Captain Oveur is paged to the white courtesy phone; he picks up the wrong phone (a red one or a standard one); the PA repeats 'No, the WHITE phone!'
jokes.setup: Captain Oveur is paged repeatedly to the 'white courtesy phone'
jokes.punchline: He picks up a non-white phone; the PA announcer has to correct him — 'No, the white phone!' — implying this obvious man cannot follow the simplest instruction
jokes.explanation: Establishes Captain Oveur as an oblivious, hapless authority figure immediately — important character work disguised as a quick visual gag. The joke doubles as early setup-and-pay for Oveur's incompetence running through the whole film. Well-structured and efficient.

jokes.text: 'Give me Hamm on five, hold the Mayo.'
jokes.setup: Captain Oveur is on an urgent call from Dr. Brody at the Mayo Clinic about a heart transplant patient; the operator interrupts saying there's an emergency call from 'Mr. Hamm' on line five
jokes.punchline: Oveur tells the operator 'Give me Hamm on five, hold the Mayo' — a deli-sandwich instruction disguised as a telephone switching command
jokes.explanation: One of Airplane!'s most celebrated one-liners. The setup is entirely 'earned' — the film takes real time establishing the Mayo Clinic call and then carefully introduces 'Mr. Hamm on five' so the punchline lands as a perfect double-meaning. The joke works on two registers simultaneously (phone etiquette and sandwich order) and requires zero additional explanation. Flawless economy (six words). The fact that it arrives in the context of a life-or-death medical emergency makes it even more transgressive. Comfortably earns 8.5+.

jokes.text: 'I haven't been able to get near a plane since the war.' / 'And they wouldn't hire me because of my war record.'
jokes.setup: Ted is explaining why he couldn't take the Boeing job — he says he hasn't been able to get near a plane 'since the war'
jokes.punchline: His second line reveals his 'war record' is what prevents him from being hired — but Elaine says everyone else considers it ancient history. The implication is Ted's war trauma is self-inflicted narrative, not fact.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy establishing Ted as a self-mythologizing loser who blames the war for everything. The joke is subtle — played as straight drama but seeded with irony ('they wouldn't hire me because of my war record'). Gets funnier in retrospect once we see his flashback. Mid-range score appropriate.

jokes.text: 'War record? You're the only one keeping that alive. For everyone else, it's ancient history.'
jokes.setup: Ted blames his war record for professional failures
jokes.punchline: Elaine deflates his self-pity with the observation that only he cares about the war record anymore — suggesting his trauma is self-constructed victimhood
jokes.explanation: Understated irony — played straight as a dramatic beat but laced with the film's mock-heroic commentary on Ted as an unironic disaster-film 'hero.' Competent but not especially funny on its own; works more as character setup.

jokes.text: Ted buys a one-way ticket to Chicago with no baggage, smoking section — played as a dramatic, quasi-suicidal gesture
jokes.setup: Ted has just watched Elaine board the plane and is determined to follow her; asks for one ticket to Chicago, 'no baggage'
jokes.punchline: The 'no baggage' and 'smoking' requests in context of a romantic pursuit read as a parody of the 'desperate romantic gesture' movie trope — played completely straight as if he's booking passage to his doom
jokes.explanation: Understated parody of the impulsive romantic-hero trope. The 'no baggage' detail is the best part — traveling with nothing as a symbol of total commitment/desperation. Not a big laugh but a knowing wink at disaster-film conventions. Functional mid-range joke.

jokes.text: Ted's war flashback: a radio command echoes endlessly — 'The decision is yours... is yours... is yours...' — establishing Ted's psychological damage via absurd audio loop
jokes.setup: Ted hears a radio call ('Striker, this is Red Leader Four. Primary target covered by fog. Decision to proceed is yours.')
jokes.punchline: The phrase 'is yours' echoes and repeats in a loop, an absurdist representation of Ted's PTSD — the traumatic moment rendered as a broken record
jokes.explanation: Clever parody of disaster-film flashback conventions — the PTSD/trauma trope rendered as a literal broken record is both funny and efficient character work. The absurdist audio loop does double duty: it's a formal joke about movie conventions and also characterizes Ted's paralysis. Good character integration.

jokes.text: In the middle of the jive conversation, one passenger solemnly declares: 'Early to bed, early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise.' / 'How true! Golly!'
jokes.setup: The jive conversation has been about conventional domestic drama (cheating neighbor, moral choices)
jokes.punchline: One passenger solemnly quotes Ben Franklin's proverb in the middle of this heated jive exchange; the other responds with 'How true! Golly!' — as if this cliché is a profound insight
jokes.explanation: Callback to the jive subtitle gag — the Ben Franklin proverb appearing as apparently sincere wisdom in the middle of this jive exchange is an escalation of the original joke's disconnect between form and content. 'How true! Golly!' as the enthusiastic response to a 250-year-old platitude seals it. Good extension of a running gag.

jokes.text: 'Nervous?' / 'Yes.' / 'First time?' / 'No. I've been nervous lots of times.'
jokes.setup: Classic romantic/nervous-flier dialogue setup: 'Nervous? First time?' — clearly asking if this is her first time flying
jokes.punchline: The passenger interprets 'First time?' as asking if this is her first time being nervous, answering 'No. I've been nervous lots of times.' — a perfectly literal non-answer that defeats the question
jokes.explanation: One of the great literalism jokes in comedy film history. The setup uses the most archetypal romantic/thriller shorthand ('Nervous? First time?') and the punchline demolishes it with perfect logic: she WAS answering the question asked, just not the question implied. This is the ZAZ literalism engine at peak efficiency — four lines, zero waste, maximum subversion. The joke earns its 8.5+ because it weaponizes a universal piece of dramatic shorthand against itself with impeccable economy.

jokes.text: Bill and his girlfriend exchange a watch as a farewell gift. 'It's your watch. You shouldn't. You're going to need this.' / 'It's all right. It doesn't work.'
jokes.setup: An emotional exchange of a watch as a sentimental farewell token — standard disaster movie trope
jokes.punchline: The sentimental watch doesn't work — deflating the emotional gesture entirely with a matter-of-fact revelation
jokes.explanation: Clean, economic deflation joke. The setup (sentimental watch exchange) is a recognizable genre beat, and 'It's all right. It doesn't work' is delivered with complete sincerity making it funnier. Good economy — the punchline is four words. The joke is that the most sentimental gestures in disaster movies are often revealed as worthless by ZAZ.

jokes.text: Tearful farewell between Bill and 'darling' at the gate — giving him a watch that 'doesn't work' as a keepsake
jokes.setup: An emotional, drawn-out airport goodbye between Bill and his partner — she gives him her watch as a parting gift
jokes.punchline: 'It's all right. It doesn't work.' — a completely useless keepsake offered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Sweet, economical joke embedded in a parody of overwrought airport farewell scenes. The broken watch is the perfect detail — she's giving something meaningless with complete earnestness. It's also a parody of the 'meaningful object' trope in melodrama. Solid mid-range joke.

jokes.text: 'We have clearance, Clarence.' / 'Roger, Roger. What's our vector, Victor?' — the pilot/co-pilot name confusion exchange
jokes.setup: Air traffic control radio communication with the cockpit, using standard aviation call signs and pilot names (Captain Clarence Oveur, First Officer Roger Murdock, Second Officer Victor Basta)
jokes.punchline: The pilots' actual names ('Clarence,' 'Roger,' 'Victor') match standard radio acknowledgment words, creating cascading confusion: 'We have clearance, Clarence' / 'Roger, Roger' / 'What's our vector, Victor?' — eventually devolving into 'Roger. / Huh? / Roger. Over. / Huh? Who?'
jokes.explanation: The single best joke of this reel and one of the most admired bits in Airplane! The setup is entirely earned by the film's earlier introduction of all three pilots by name — this is the payoff of a long, patient setup that most audiences don't even notice. The wordplay cascade is structurally perfect: each exchange adds a layer of confusion while remaining individually comprehensible, the whole thing escalating until communication itself breaks down. The character integration is exceptional — the pilots' names are not incidental; they were chosen specifically for this moment. 'Roger, Roger. What's our vector, Victor?' is as quotable as film comedy gets. Easily earns 9+ across the board.

jokes.text: Passenger asks for something to read; stewardess offers a leaflet titled 'Famous Jewish Sports Legends'
jokes.setup: Passenger asks stewardess, 'Would you like something to read? Do you have anything light?'
jokes.punchline: 'How about this leaflet, "Famous Jewish Sports Legends"?' — a spectacularly thin pamphlet that is 'light' only in the sense of being brief, implying Jewish sports legends are few
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ misdirection/literalism: 'anything light' is answered with literal lightness (a thin pamphlet) but the actual joke is the specific title — a thin pamphlet on a topic stereotyped as sparse. The joke works both as literalism (light = not heavy to read) and as self-deprecating Jewish humor. Clean double-meaning structure with excellent economy.

jokes.text: Older male passenger watches Elaine walk away and comments: 'No wonder you're upset. She's lovely. And a darling figure. Supple, pouting breasts, firm thighs. It's a shame you two don't get along.'
jokes.setup: Ted is visibly upset that Elaine (the stewardess) is brushing him off; an older male passenger beside him takes in the situation
jokes.punchline: Instead of offering comfort or sage advice, the passenger launches into an increasingly detailed physical appraisal of Elaine's body, then concludes with the mild understatement 'It's a shame you two don't get along' — as if his leering was sympathetic support
jokes.explanation: The joke's structure is the gap between expected (sympathy, advice) and actual (lecherous commentary) — the escalation into 'supple, pouting breasts, firm thighs' and then the pivot to polite understatement is very ZAZ. The oblivious creepiness played as good-natured support is funny. Solid mid-upper range.

jokes.text: 'It was worse than Detroit.'
jokes.setup: Ted is narrating his wartime backstory — describing the bar where he met Elaine: 'the seediest dive on the wharf, populated with every reject and cut-throat from Bombay to Calcutta'
jokes.punchline: 'It was worse than Detroit.' — an offhand, contemporary American municipal insult dropped into the midst of an exotic wartime adventure narrative
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical anachronism/bathos — the whole rhythm of the exotic adventure description ('Bombay to Calcutta') is punctured by the casual American civic burn. Five words, maximum deflation. The joke trusts the audience to get the tonal whiplash without any additional signposting. This is exactly what deadpan understatement should do.

jokes.text: Ted's wartime bar flashback — the entire bar brawl background action while Ted narrates lovingly about meeting Elaine
jokes.setup: Ted narrates in voiceover about the rough bar ('a fight broke out almost every night') while we see the actual scene play out
jokes.punchline: The background of the bar is filled with increasingly absurd slapstick violence, exotic dancing, and mayhem that escalates completely independently of Ted's romantic narration — the visual track and audio track are in total comic disconnection
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ audio/visual disconnection gag — the earnest romantic narration over increasingly chaotic, absurd background action is a sustained visual comedy set piece. Earns rewatch bonus because new details emerge each viewing. The technique of using the narrator's straight delivery as a foil for insane visuals is a ZAZ specialty executed well here.

jokes.text: 'I had to asked this guy to pinch me to make sure I wasn't dreaming.'
jokes.setup: Ted is narrating his romantic awakening when he first saw Elaine: 'I was captivated, entranced. It hit me like a thunderbolt.'
jokes.punchline: Instead of a poetic cliché about the moment, he describes literally asking a stranger to pinch him — a mundane, awkward action that punctures the romantic grandeur
jokes.explanation: Functional bathos — the romantic build ('captivated, entranced, hit me like a thunderbolt') is deflated by the literal, awkward physical reality of asking a stranger to pinch him. The grammar error ('I had to asked') is likely intentional, adding to Ted's hapless charm. Solid mid-range joke.

jokes.text: Whenever I talk about Elaine, I get carried away. I lose all track of time.
jokes.setup: Ted has apparently been talking for an extremely long time
jokes.punchline: His understatement about 'losing track of time' implies he has talked so long his seatmate has died — the gap in timestamps (21:22 to 21:33) suggests a very long monologue compressed
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of Ted's deadly boring storytelling. Functional but secondary to the visual payoff (the dead seatmate). Works in context, slight on its own.

jokes.text: When can I see the cockpit? / The pilots are probably too busy flying the plane for that.
jokes.setup: Joey (a boy) asks to see the cockpit, a reasonable request; the attendant gives a sensible discouraging answer
jokes.punchline: The punchline is structural — the film immediately cuts to the cockpit where Joey is taken, and the captain proceeds to ask him highly inappropriate questions, making the attendant's reassurance ironic
jokes.explanation: Setup joke whose payoff is structural — the irony of the attendant's reassurance lands on rewatch when you know what happens in the cockpit. Modest on first viewing.

jokes.text: "No, I take it black. Like my men."
jokes.setup: Stewardess offers cream for coffee — a mundane, polite exchange aboard the plane.
jokes.punchline: The passenger's addendum 'Like my men' recontextualizes 'black' as a statement about her sexual preferences, delivered with total deadpan calm.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker economy. Four words do all the work. The setup is completely innocent, the pivot is instant and unexpected, and the deadpan delivery makes it land harder. It's one of the film's most quotable beats — perfectly structured misdirection with maximum payoff per syllable. Scores 8+ because it's genuinely exceptional: nothing telegraphed, nothing wasted.

jokes.text: Captain Oveur asks Joey, "Have you ever seen a grown man naked?"
jokes.setup: Joey is a wide-eyed boy invited into the cockpit as a special treat. The captain is being hospitable.
jokes.punchline: Oveur asks a deeply inappropriate question — sexual in implication — in the most matter-of-fact, polite tone possible.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's signature running gags and a showcase for the ZAZ method: total deadpan incongruity. The escalating series of inappropriate questions to a child is pure character comedy — Oveur exists only to ask these questions, and the character is inseparable from the joke. Scores 8+ for tight structure, complete character integration, shocking audacity executed with perfect economy, and genuine cultural staying power.

jokes.text: Captain Oveur asks Joey, "Do you ever hang around a gymnasium?"
jokes.setup: Following the 'grown man naked' question, Oveur switches to another inappropriate inquiry delivered with equal innocence.
jokes.punchline: The question itself — implying Oveur frequents or expects Joey to frequent gyms for predatory reasons — escalates the running gag.
jokes.explanation: The second beat in the Oveur/Joey running gag. Slightly weaker than the original because it no longer has the element of surprise, but the escalation and character consistency keep it funny. The seemingly innocuous phrasing layered over obvious inappropriate subtext is the ZAZ formula working well.

jokes.text: Joey tells 'Roger Murdock' that his dad says he doesn't work hard enough on defense, doesn't run downcourt, and doesn't try except during playoffs — and Kareem breaks character: "The hell I don't! Listen, kid, I've been hearing that crap ever since I was at UCLA..."
jokes.setup: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar is playing 'co-pilot Roger Murdock' and insists he is not Kareem. Joey, undeterred, relays his dad's criticism of Kareem's defense.
jokes.punchline: Kareem completely drops the pretense and defends himself with genuine NBA-player indignation, referencing UCLA, Bill Walton, Bob Lanier — the fiction collapses entirely.
jokes.explanation: Among the best jokes in the film. The conceit — casting the actual Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as a pilot who insists he's not Kareem — is already clever, but the payoff where a child's dad-relayed sports criticism makes him abandon all pretense is inspired. It's purely character-specific: no other actor or athlete could replace Kareem here. The specificity of the defense statistics, Walton, Lanier, and UCLA elevates it far beyond a generic celebrity cameo gag. Scores 8+ comfortably — exceptional originality, perfect character integration, and genuine comedic escalation.

jokes.text: Captain Oveur to Joey: "Do you like movies about gladiators?"
jokes.setup: After Kareem's outburst, the cockpit settles. Oveur resumes his avuncular manner with the boy.
jokes.punchline: The question — implying gladiator-themed homoerotic entertainment — continues the escalating pattern of Oveur's inappropriate questions, now with a pop-culture twist.
jokes.explanation: The third and arguably funniest of the Oveur questions in this reel. 'Movies about gladiators' is more absurd and culturally specific than the previous two, and by now the audience has the pattern — but ZAZ subverts expectations by picking the most oblique possible phrasing. Very high quotability; this line has genuine cultural longevity. Scores 8+ because the economy is perfect (five words, entirely implicit) and the character integration remains total.

jokes.text: Elaine's flashback monologue: "I remember how you used to hold me, and how I used to sit on your face and wriggle..." followed by an innocent continuation about watching the sunrise.
jokes.setup: Elaine narrates a tender romantic memory with Ted — intimate, nostalgic phrasing about being held.
jokes.punchline: "I used to sit on your face and wriggle" — delivered with complete sincerity as part of a romantic reverie, then pivoting immediately to the innocent image of watching the sunrise together.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ construction: a character says something sexually explicit while clearly meaning something innocent (or not — the script is deliberately ambiguous), delivered with zero self-awareness. The pivot to watching the sunrise reinforces that Elaine experiences no dissonance. The long romantic windup makes the drop land harder. Strong originality score because the phrasing is specific and the innocent-continuation structure is well-engineered.

jokes.text: "Headquarters? What is it?" / "A big building where generals meet, but that's not important."
jokes.setup: Someone says 'You got a telegram from headquarters today.' Ted asks 'What is it?' — a standard question meaning 'What does it say?'
jokes.punchline: The respondent answers the literal meaning of 'what is it' — describing headquarters as a building — then dismisses it: 'but that's not important.'
jokes.explanation: The first deployment of ZAZ's signature 'literalism' gag — answering a rhetorical or idiomatic question with a literal definition, then adding 'but that's not important' to deflect. It's structurally brilliant: the dismissal is both a punchline and a meta-acknowledgment that the literalism is the joke. High quotability because the formula is instantly replicable by audiences. Scores well because it's a crisp, original execution of an idea that becomes a recurring motif in the film.

jokes.text: "I wish I could say the same for George Zip." — Ted's non-sequitur callback to a dead soldier named George Zip whenever someone says something hopeful.
jokes.setup: Elaine or the nurse says something encouraging about Ted's recovery. Ted responds solemnly.
jokes.punchline: 'I wish I could say the same for George Zip' — a morose callback to an apparently dead soldier, used to undercut every optimistic statement.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed running gag that works as both character comedy (Ted's paralysing survivor guilt) and absurdist deflation. The name 'George Zip' is itself funny — specific enough to feel real, silly enough to register as comedy. The callback structure is tight because the setup (Zip dying) occurred only moments earlier in this same scene.

jokes.text: "Hey, Striker, how about a break? I'm getting tired." — a background patient who has apparently been listening to Ted's endless story breaks character.
jokes.setup: Ted has been monologuing about his war guilt and personal history. The scene is played straight.
jokes.punchline: A random patient in the ward — who has apparently been an involuntary audience — asks for a break because he's tired of listening.
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-joke that acknowledges the audience's own potential fatigue with Ted's self-pitying monologue. The randomness of the character (a stranger who has nothing to do with the scene) is the source of absurdity. 'Take five' as a response — treating it like a work break — adds a secondary layer. Good originality score because the meta angle is genuinely unexpected.

jokes.text: The 'wonderful apartment' description is interrupted by a war flashback: "Red Leader! Red Leader, I'm going down!"
jokes.setup: Elaine describes a lovely apartment she found — fireplace, cute bedroom with mirrors on the ceiling — a romantic domestic scene.
jokes.punchline: A psychiatric patient bursts in with a full WWII air-battle hallucination, completely derailing the tender moment.
jokes.explanation: A solid absurdist interruption gag. The contrast between Elaine's domestic sweetness and the patient's combat mania is well-timed. The mirrors-on-the-ceiling detail also adds a subtle innuendo to the setup that makes the interruption doubly deflating. Functional, good timing, but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "$25 for a cigarette is too much!" — shouted by a hallucinating patient mid-combat delusion.
jokes.setup: A patient is mid-combat hallucination, shouting military commands.
jokes.punchline: The hallucination randomly pivots to a mundane consumer complaint — the price of a cigarette — before presumably returning to the battle.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist non-sequitur that gets its laugh from the extreme tonal whiplash. The specific price point ($25) anchors it in comic specificity rather than pure randomness. Mildly funny — it's a quick gag that doesn't overstay its welcome.

jokes.text: "It's Lieutenant Hurwitz. Severe shell shock. He thinks he's Ethel Merman."
jokes.setup: Staff member explains the behavior of an erratic patient to Ted.
jokes.punchline: The patient's delusion is not that he's Napoleon, a general, or even another soldier — but Ethel Merman, Broadway belter.
jokes.explanation: The punchline is entirely in the name 'Ethel Merman.' The specificity is what makes it exceptional — not just a singer or a woman, but *Ethel Merman*, the most theatrically outsized Broadway diva imaginable. The gap between 'traumatized soldier' and 'Ethel Merman' is enormous and inherently comic. The deadpan clinical delivery ('He thinks he's...') perfectly frames the absurdity. High originality because the choice of Merman is genuinely inspired.

jokes.text: The patient actually IS performing as Ethel Merman — a full belting Broadway performance in the psychiatric ward — followed by "War is hell."
jokes.setup: We've been told the patient thinks he's Ethel Merman. The film then presumably shows/implies the full theatrical performance.
jokes.punchline: "War is hell." — a solemn, clichéd war-movie closing line used to punctuate the most absurd scene in the hospital sequence.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke. First: the visual payoff of the patient actually performing is itself the visual gag, committed to fully. Second: 'War is hell' as the capper is a perfect example of ZAZ's ability to weaponize sincerity — using a dead-serious cliché as a punchline to the most ridiculous sequence. The juxtaposition of Merman's showstopper with that four-word gravitas is structurally elegant. Scores 8+ for structure, economy, and the audacity of commitment.

jokes.text: "Jim never has a second cup of coffee at home." — repeated by a wife when her husband asks for a second cup.
jokes.setup: Jim asks for a second cup of coffee — a trivial domestic action.
jokes.punchline: His wife's comment frames this mild indulgence as a notable deviation from home behavior, as if it's remarkable and slightly alarming.
jokes.explanation: A recurring ZAZ gag — the wife who comments on Jim's behavior as though reporting to an authority. The joke is in the specificity and the total mundaneness of the observation. The 'Jim never...' construction is the whole joke. It's also a setup for the vomiting callback later in the reel, making it structurally significant. Good deadpan economy.

jokes.text: Randy borrows a guitar and goes to cheer up the sick girl Lisa — the film then plays a lengthy performance sequence.
jokes.setup: Randy sincerely wants to cheer up a sick child with a guitar song. Sweet and wholesome setup.
jokes.punchline: The performance goes on for an extended, earnest duration — the joke is the commitment to the bit and the uncomfortable awkwardness of the extended 'cheer-up' sequence, culminating in Randy accidentally knocking the sick girl's IV or medical equipment (implied by the extended time gap to [33:00]).
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most celebrated extended gags. The setup is heartwarming; the execution is a full, committed musical performance that escalates into physical chaos (Randy hits the sick girl with the guitar and knocks over her equipment, as implied by the gap to 33:00 and film knowledge). The commitment to the bit — playing it completely straight while chaos escalates — is classic ZAZ. The extended duration is the point: economy is sacrificed deliberately for maximum discomfort payoff. Scores high for structure and originality of execution.

jokes.text: Ted and Elaine's Peace Corps assignment: introducing the isolated Molombos tribe to 'western culture' — which turns out to be a Tupperware party.
jokes.setup: Ted narrates gravely about introducing an isolated tribe to 'our western culture' — implying education, democracy, modern agriculture.
jokes.punchline: What they were actually introduced to was a Tupperware demonstration — a housewife sales pitch for plastic food containers.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel. The satirical gap between 'western civilization' and 'Tupperware party' is enormous and precisely chosen. The narration is played with complete earnestness — no wink — while the visual contradiction (tribal people watching a home products demo) does all the comedic work. It's also a sharp piece of cultural satire about American imperialism disguised as a pure sight gag. Scores 8+ for genuine originality, perfect structure, and layered meaning.

jokes.text: Ted's Peace Corps 'athletic program' for the Molombos — calisthenics, game skills, 'advanced competitive theory' — culminating in the tribe playing basketball.
jokes.setup: Ted narrates seriously about introducing an isolated people to 'physical fitness' and 'athletic equipment' using 'advanced American teaching techniques.'
jokes.punchline: The tribe is playing full-court basketball — a visual non-sequitur that also (given the Kareem gag earlier) adds a thematic resonance with the basketball subplot.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that works on multiple levels: the absurdity of colonial 'uplift' producing a basketball game, the earnest narration, and the callback resonance with the Kareem storyline. The specificity of 'advanced competitive theory' in the narration is a nice detail. Good but not exceptional — the Tupperware joke in the same sequence is stronger.

jokes.text: "A lot of people made plans before the war. Like George Zip."
jokes.setup: Elaine says it's time to go home and pursue the plans they made before the war.
jokes.punchline: Ted invokes George Zip again — the dead soldier — as a counterpoint to making plans, with tragic deadpan.
jokes.explanation: The second George Zip callback. Works slightly better here because the setup ('plans before the war') makes George Zip's death more thematically apt as a counterpoint. The escalating deployment of this running gag across multiple scenes demonstrates good structural awareness from the writers.

jokes.text: "I haven't felt this awful since we saw that Ronald Reagan film."
jokes.setup: A passenger feels ill. He's looking for context for how bad he feels.
jokes.punchline: The reference point for peak awfulness in his life is a Ronald Reagan film — a pointed jab at Reagan as an actor (Reagan was then U.S. president, 1980).
jokes.explanation: A topical political joke that works because of its understatement — it's delivered as a casual personal reference, not a punchline. In 1980, with Reagan just elected president, the joke has an extra sting. The structure is good (simile as punchline), though it's slightly character-agnostic. Good impact score for the period audience.

jokes.text: Captain Oveur to Joey: "Joey, have you ever been in a Turkish prison?"
jokes.setup: The cockpit is now dealing with a medical emergency. Oveur is briefly interrupted from crisis management.
jokes.punchline: He resumes his series of inappropriate questions to Joey — this time referencing Turkish prisons, implying sexual imprisonment scenarios.
jokes.explanation: The fourth Oveur question and arguably the most culturally durable. 'Have you ever been in a Turkish prison?' has become one of the film's most quoted lines. By this point the audience anticipates the gag but the specific wording still surprises — Turkish prison implies a very particular kind of threat. The fact that it arrives in the middle of a crisis (Oveur briefly returning to inappropriate small talk) adds absurdist context. High quotability.

jokes.text: "Jim never vomits at home."
jokes.setup: Jim (presumably) vomits due to food poisoning. His wife observes.
jokes.punchline: She repeats the 'Jim never does X at home' formula — applied now to vomiting, which makes the mundane domestic framing grotesquely funny.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the 'Jim never...' running gag, and it's a perfect escalation. The formula 'Jim never X at home' worked mildly for coffee; applied to vomiting it becomes genuinely funny because the gap between the mundane domestic framework and the disgusting action is enormous. The callback structure is tight — same phrasing, catastrophically different subject. Scores 8+ for structure and economy; six words do enormous comedic work.

jokes.text: "A hospital! What is it?" / "It's a big building with patients, but that's not important."
jokes.setup: Doctor says the passenger must go to a hospital. Someone reacts with 'A hospital! What is it?' — using the idiomatic sense.
jokes.punchline: Second deployment of the literalism formula: 'It's a big building with patients, but that's not important.'
jokes.explanation: The running gag's second deployment, now escalated to a crisis context. The 'but that's not important' dismissal is funnier here because there IS something important going on. The formula is well-established enough that the audience is now anticipating it, which makes the delivery of 'with patients' feel like a satisfying inevitable. Good running gag mechanics.

jokes.text: "Can't you take a guess?" / "Not for another two hours." — Oveur literally cannot estimate the landing time, interpreted as being unable to even guess.
jokes.setup: Doctor asks 'Can't you take a guess?' about the landing time. Standard urgent question.
jokes.punchline: Oveur answers as if the doctor is asking about his ability to speculate: 'Not for another two hours' — meaning he won't have enough information to guess until then, but it sounds like he's incapable of guessing for two hours.
jokes.explanation: A quick literalism gag that works on a double reading of 'take a guess.' Clean and efficient, though not as crisp as the 'headquarters' or 'hospital' versions. Gets a mild laugh from the ambiguity.

jokes.text: "I haven't seen anything like this since the Anita Bryant Concert."
jokes.setup: Doctor is asked what's going on with the sick passengers. He needs a reference point for mass illness.
jokes.punchline: His reference is the Anita Bryant Concert — implying that attending an Anita Bryant show is itself a sickening experience. (Anita Bryant was a polarizing anti-gay activist in the late 1970s.)
jokes.explanation: Similar structure to the Reagan joke — a celebrity reference as a simile for maximum awfulness. The Anita Bryant choice is sharper because she was more viscerally controversial in 1980 (her anti-gay campaign was recent and raw), and the medical context (mass sickness) makes the comparison more pointed. Good topical joke with solid construction.

jokes.text: "What did we have for dinner?" / "We had a choice — steak or fish." / "Yes, I remember. I had Lasagna."
jokes.setup: Doctor urgently asks what the sick passengers ate. The stewardess confirms: steak or fish.
jokes.punchline: A passenger volunteers that he had Lasagna — a meal that was not on offer, delivered with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: A deceptively simple gag that lands hard because of its total commitment. The passenger is not joking — he genuinely believes he had lasagna. The contradiction (there was no lasagna) is delivered with zero acknowledgment from anyone. This is pure ZAZ deadpan: the world does not stop to point out the absurdity. High marks for structure and economy.

jokes.text: What did we have for dinner? / We had a choice — steak or fish. / Yes, I remember. I had Lasagna.
jokes.setup: Doctor urgently asks what the sick passengers had for dinner to identify the cause; attendant says 'steak or fish'
jokes.punchline: A random passenger interjects 'Yes, I remember. I had Lasagna' — there was no lasagna option, making his contribution both useless and inexplicable
jokes.explanation: Perfect absurdist interruption. The lasagna man helpfully contributes information that is both specific (he remembers exactly what he had) and completely irrelevant (there was no lasagna). The sincerity of the delivery is crucial — he genuinely thinks he's being helpful. Tight, surprising, and characteristically Airplane!.

jokes.text: "Put it on... automatic pilot." — followed by the reveal that the automatic pilot is a literal inflatable dummy.
jokes.setup: Pilot instructs someone to engage the automatic pilot — a standard aviation command.
jokes.punchline: The 'automatic pilot' (Otto) is revealed to be a literal inflatable human dummy in the co-pilot's seat — a visual gag that the film will pay off extensively.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's iconic gags. The literalism of 'automatic pilot' — a staple of ZAZ — is here executed as a full physical prop. The idea of an inflatable man as the backup system for a 707 is both brilliantly absurd and structurally perfect as a visual gag that will generate more jokes throughout the film. Scores 8+ for genuine originality, strong structure, and high rewatch/setup value.

jokes.text: Put it on... automatic pilot. / Automatic pilot, automatic pilot... There it is!
jokes.setup: The captain is incapacitated; someone needs to engage the autopilot in this emergency
jokes.punchline: The 'automatic pilot' is a literal inflatable man — 'Otto' — a physical dummy that the crew has to inflate and physically seat at the controls (inferred from later dialogue about inflation nozzle)
jokes.explanation: One of the film's great visual concepts — 'autopilot' taken literally as an inflatable pilot dummy. The setup is in the dialogue ('there it is!') and the visual payoff is 'Otto,' who becomes a recurring character. The literalism device that runs through the film applied to a visual/physical gag is excellent. High originality for the concept.

jokes.text: McCroskey: "Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit smoking."
jokes.setup: McCroskey is managing an escalating crisis at Chicago air control. He's under massive pressure.
jokes.punchline: He mutters that he picked the wrong week to quit smoking — a self-pitying, banal personal complaint inserted into a catastrophic professional crisis.
jokes.explanation: The first deployment of the film's most beloved running gag. Lloyd Bridges as McCroskey delivers this with perfect flat affect — it's entirely character-specific (a man whose coping mechanisms are destroying him), structurally immaculate, and incredibly quotable. The bathos of placing a minor personal vice complaint into an aviation catastrophe is the entire joke, and it works because of commitment and economy. Scores 8+ for quotability, character integration, and the fact that it became a cultural touchstone.

jokes.text: Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit smoking.
jokes.setup: McCroskey is in the middle of a full crisis — multiple sick passengers, no pilots, fog closing airports — and is under enormous pressure
jokes.punchline: He mutters 'Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit smoking' — the first deployment of his escalating bad-week-to-quit running gag
jokes.explanation: Introduction of one of the film's great running gags. The line works perfectly on its own as a deadpan understatement — a catastrophic plane emergency reduced to an inconvenient context for quitting smoking. The structure is impeccable: huge stakes, tiny personal complaint. The 'wrong week to quit' construction is endlessly repeatable (and the film will repeat it with escalating substances). Highly quotable, strong character specificity. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: "Get the best available man who won't crack under pressure." / "How about Mr Rogers?" / "Get me Rex Kramer."
jokes.setup: McCroskey asks for the best, most pressure-resistant man available.
jokes.punchline: Staff suggests 'Mr Rogers' — presumably the gentle children's TV host Mr Rogers — before McCroskey dismisses it and calls for Rex Kramer.
jokes.explanation: A quick pop-culture joke suggesting Mr Rogers — the most famously gentle and unflappable man in America — as a crisis responder. The gap between the job requirements ('won't crack under pressure') and Mr Rogers is delicious. Clean setup and instant deflation. Would score higher with more originality, but the joke is essentially just the juxtaposition of the name.

jokes.text: "On his belt line there's a hollow tube. That's the manual inflation nozzle. Pull it out and blow on it."
jokes.setup: Elaine is told how to re-inflate the automatic pilot in clinical, technical terms.
jokes.punchline: The instructions — locating a 'hollow tube' at the 'belt line' and blowing on it — are anatomically suggestive, delivered in the most straight-faced instructional tone possible.
jokes.explanation: A supremely well-constructed double-entendre that works because every word is technically accurate for inflating a rubber dummy AND sexually suggestive simultaneously. The script never winks — ground control is entirely earnest. This is ZAZ at its most precise: each word choice is deliberate, the clinical register amplifies the impropriety, and the visual of Elaine following these instructions is the final payoff. Scores 8+ for structure and economy.

jokes.text: Doctor asks Elaine if she can face some unpleasant facts. She answers flatly: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Doctor solemnly asks Elaine, as a crew member, if she can 'face some unpleasant facts' — implying bravery and professionalism are required.
jokes.punchline: Elaine answers simply 'No.' — the most unheroic possible response delivered without affect.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ literalism/deflation. The setup demands a heroic answer; the monosyllabic 'No' punctures it completely. The economy is near-perfect — one word does all the work. Earns a high craft score for precision.

jokes.text: Doctor: 'Our lives depend on just one thing — finding someone to fly this plane who didn't have fish for dinner.'
jokes.setup: Doctor delivers a grave speech about the stakes: 'Our lives depend on just one thing—' implying something dramatic like skill, courage, or radio contact.
jokes.punchline: The 'one thing' is mundanely logistical: finding someone who didn't eat the fish.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured misdirection: heroic phrasing collapses into bureaucratic specificity. The callback to the fish poisoning grounds it in the film's internal logic, making it feel earned rather than random.

jokes.text: Elaine's PA: 'We regret any inconvenience the sudden cabin movement caused. This is due to periodic air pockets.'
jokes.setup: The plane is in full crisis — people are gravely ill, pilots are incapacitated.
jokes.punchline: The official PA announcement describes the chaos as a minor 'sudden cabin movement' caused by 'periodic air pockets' — catastrophic understatement.
jokes.explanation: Solid institutional-speak understatement gag. Works as satirical commentary on airline communication culture but isn't particularly surprising at this point in the film.

jokes.text: Elaine ends the routine PA announcement with: 'By the way, is there anyone on board who can fly a plane?'
jokes.setup: Elaine delivers a perfectly calm, reassuring PA address — 'no reason to become alarmed, enjoy your flight.'
jokes.punchline: She then casually appends the desperate, life-or-death request for a pilot as though it's an afterthought ('By the way...').
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes. The structure is immaculate: lull audience into the mundane PA rhythm, then detonate with the most urgent possible question delivered in the most casual possible register. 'By the way' is doing enormous comedic heavy lifting. Highly quotable and a genuine laugh-out-loud moment.

jokes.text: Visual gag: Captain Kramer's home — a man named Paul Carey arrives to pick up 'Captain Kramer,' and a large, excitable dog named Shep repeatedly misbehaves while the humans discuss the emergency.
jokes.setup: Grave airline emergency conversation is conducted in a domestic setting.
jokes.punchline: The dog Shep keeps interrupting the serious discussion — 'Shep, sit! Sit!', 'Shep, no!', 'Shep! Come!' — undercutting the tension with mundane pet chaos.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ tonal collision — mortal stakes discussed while a dog acts up. It's not especially original but executed with good comic rhythm across three beats ('Sit!', 'No!', 'Come!'). The escalation across the scene elevates it slightly.

jokes.text: Kramer's tirade about FAA and airlines: 'they're all cheats and liars.'
jokes.setup: Paul Carey asks Kramer about food inspection failures on flights; Kramer builds to an institutional critique.
jokes.punchline: He concludes with the blunt, undiplomatic 'they're all cheats and liars' — from an airline captain, the ultimate insider condemnation, delivered deadpan before abruptly ending: 'All right. Let's get out of here.'
jokes.explanation: Decent character comedy — Kramer's blunt contempt for his own industry is funny partly because of Lloyd Bridges's earnest delivery in the film and partly because it subverts the authority figure trope. Not especially original but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Transition to airport — a man in the terminal appears to be pitching his terrible infrastructure story to anyone who will listen, then continues rambling about jeeps, broken axles, and drainage.
jokes.setup: In what appears to be a search for a qualified pilot in the terminal, Elaine or someone approaches a passenger.
jokes.punchline: The man launches into an irrelevant, exhausting monologue about roads, drainage, and jeep breakdowns — completely ignoring the life-or-death context.
jokes.explanation: A riff on the oblivious bore who can't read a room. The specificity of the rambling (axles, drainage, jeeps) is in ZAZ's wheelhouse of absurd commitment, but the gag runs slightly long without enough escalation.

jokes.text: 'Excuse me, sir. There's a problem in the cockpit.' / 'The cockpit? What is it?' / 'The little room where the pilot sits. That's not important.'
jokes.setup: Elaine urgently says there's 'a problem in the cockpit.' The man asks 'What is it?' — intending 'what's the problem?'
jokes.punchline: She answers the literal question: 'The little room where the pilot sits' — then brushes past it as if she said nothing notable: 'That's not important.'
jokes.explanation: One of the great ZAZ literalism jokes. The 'what is it?' question has two valid grammatical readings; she answers the wrong one with perfect deadpan, then dismisses it with 'That's not important.' The triple-layered structure (setup → literal answer → dismissal) is immaculate. Economy is essentially perfect. Among the best jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: 'Surely, you can't be serious.' / 'I am serious, and don't call me Shirley.'
jokes.setup: Striker, incredulous, says 'Surely, you can't be serious' — using 'surely' as an intensifier.
jokes.punchline: Rumack takes 'Surely' as a name: 'I am serious, and don't call me Shirley.' Perfect homophone pun delivered with absolute straight-faced commitment.
jokes.explanation: The most famous joke in Airplane! and one of the most quoted lines in film comedy history. Its craft is flawless: the setup is entirely naturalistic, the punchline requires zero explanation, the name 'Shirley' is a perfect homophone, and Leslie Nielsen's straight delivery makes it legendary. It earns a 9+ on craft because there is simply no better way to construct this joke — it has been referenced, parodied, and quoted for 40+ years. This is what a 10/10 impact looks like.

jokes.text: 'It's an entirely different kind of flying... altogether.' [beat] 'It's an entirely different kind of flying.'
jokes.setup: Rumack explains that four-engine planes are different from fighters: 'It's an entirely different kind of flying... altogether.'
jokes.punchline: After the dramatic pause on 'altogether,' a second voice (or the same character) blankly repeats the whole sentence: 'It's an entirely different kind of flying.' The 'altogether' was the emphasis, and the echo strips that away.
jokes.explanation: A clever structural joke where the 'altogether' is set up as a dramatic flourish, then the follow-up repeat deflates by omitting what made it meaningful — or by being so deadpan the repetition itself is the absurdity. It's a callback pattern that the ZAZ team uses to great effect.

jokes.text: McCroskey barking airport emergency orders, then: 'It's your wife.' He pivots to domestic household instructions: 'Kids in bed by nine, dog fed, yard watered, gate locked. Get a note to the milkman — No more cheese.'
jokes.setup: McCroskey is a commanding authority figure issuing rapid-fire crisis commands to his airport team.
jokes.punchline: His wife calls and he seamlessly pivots to equally terse domestic commands, treating household chores with identical military precision — culminating in the absurd 'No more cheese.'
jokes.explanation: Superb character comedy. McCroskey's command voice is established, then immediately repurposed for the mundane. The escalating specificity of the domestic list (kids, dog, yard, gate, milkman) builds well, and 'No more cheese' is a perfectly absurd final beat — specific enough to be funny, unexplained enough to be baffling. Lloyd Bridges plays it completely straight. One of the reel's strongest jokes.

jokes.text: 'A passenger is going to land that plane.' / 'Is that possible?' / 'It's a hundred to one shot.'
jokes.setup: McCroskey reveals a civilian passenger will attempt to land the plane.
jokes.punchline: Instead of 'Yes' or 'No,' the response is 'It's a hundred to one shot' — framing a life-or-death situation in gambling odds, which both understates and darkens it.
jokes.explanation: A solid dark-comedy beat. The betting-odds framing of human survival is bleakly funny. Competent but not exceptional — the joke relies on the absurdity of the phrasing rather than any deep structure.

jokes.text: Striker reads off cockpit checklist: 'Altitude, 24,000 feet. Level flight. Speed, 520 knots. Course Zero Niner Zero. Trim, mixture. Wash, soap, rinse, spin.'
jokes.setup: Striker reads through authentic-sounding aviation checklist items with serious concentration.
jokes.punchline: The list seamlessly transitions into laundry instructions ('Wash, soap, rinse, spin') as though they're the same category.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant list joke. The aviation jargon is convincingly real for three items, then 'Wash, soap, rinse, spin' drops in with the exact same rhythm and cadence — the audience doesn't see it coming because the pattern is so well established. The commitment to the same vocal register is what makes it land. High craft for economy and structure.

jokes.text: Ted tells the concerned parties he 'can't fly this plane.' / 'That's what I'm trying to tell them.' — Ted is talking to them directly.
jokes.setup: Someone says 'You can't fly this plane!' in alarm.
jokes.punchline: Ted calmly agrees: 'That's what I'm trying to tell them' — his tone suggests he's been trying to communicate his own incompetence, treating his disqualification as a miscommunication problem rather than a crisis.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Striker's hapless self-awareness is funny precisely because he frames his own disqualification as a communication breakdown rather than a cause for despair. Tight and well-delivered.

jokes.text: 'Mayday! Mayday!' / 'Mayday? What the hell is that?' / 'May Day's the Russian new year. We'll have a big parade and serve...'
jokes.setup: Striker transmits a 'Mayday' distress call — standard aviation emergency language.
jokes.punchline: Johnny, the airport assistant, mishears/misinterprets 'Mayday' as the first of May (May Day) — and launches into plans for a Russian parade and food, derailing the emergency completely.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ literalism/wordplay. 'Mayday' has two meanings; Johnny takes the wrong one with absolute confidence. The cut-off ('and serve...') adds to the absurdism by suggesting the parade and food service were continuing. Johnny's character (clueless, well-meaning) makes this feel specific rather than generic.

jokes.text: Panicking passenger sequence: someone screaming to get off; a calm nun slaps them; a line of people forms with increasingly dramatic implements (boxing gloves, etc.) to also slap the hysterical passenger.
jokes.setup: A passenger has a breakdown and needs to be calmed down.
jokes.punchline: The 'calming down' escalates from a slap to a full queue of people waiting with boxing gloves, a baseball bat, etc. — each more extreme than the last.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's iconic visual gags. The escalation structure is perfectly engineered: each new person in line is funnier and more absurd than the last. The nun's initial slap subverts expectations (authority figure + violence), and the subsequent queue transforms individual violence into a social institution. High impact because it plays so well visually.

jokes.text: In the airport, amid the chaos, various solicitors approach people: Hare Krishnas, Reverend Moon followers, Jews for Jesus, Jehovah's Witnesses, Buddhists, Jerry's Kids, Scientology, nuclear power advocates.
jokes.setup: Airport terminal is in crisis mode; people are panicking.
jokes.punchline: A rotating carousel of religious and cause-based solicitors hits up everyone in sequence — the sheer number and variety is the joke, with each new group stranger than the last.
jokes.explanation: Airport solicitor satire that works through sheer accumulation and variety. The 1980 cultural specificity (Reverend Moon, Jerry's Kids) adds flavor. 'Nuclear power?' as the final entry is a deliberately bathos-laden closer. Not deep but efficiently executed.

jokes.text: PA announcement: 'Your attention, please. No-frills passengers now arriving. Please have your baggage claim checks ready to show upon leaving the terminal.'
jokes.setup: The airport is in full emergency mode — a plane is in crisis, people are panicking.
jokes.punchline: A completely routine, oblivious baggage claim announcement plays over the chaos as though nothing unusual is happening.
jokes.explanation: Functional institutional-obliviousness gag. 'No-frills passengers' is a mild satirical dig, but the joke is mostly tonal contrast (bureaucratic calm vs. emergency) rather than anything structurally inventive.

jokes.text: McCroskey: 'This guy has no airline experience. He's a menace to everything in the air.' / Other voice: 'Yes, birds, too.'
jokes.setup: McCroskey says Striker is a menace 'to everything in the air.'
jokes.punchline: 'Yes, birds, too.' — literally extending the metaphor to encompass wildlife, which both agrees with McCroskey and renders his severity ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do enormous work. 'Birds, too' is an absurd literal extension of a hyperbolic statement that makes the hyperbole suddenly feel understated. Johnny's consistent clueless-literalism character makes this feel grounded.

jokes.text: McCroskey: 'I took the wrong week to quit drinking.'
jokes.setup: The crisis deepens; McCroskey is under enormous stress.
jokes.punchline: He mutters that he 'took the wrong week to quit drinking' — implying he had recently made a wholesome self-improvement decision at the worst possible moment.
jokes.explanation: First installment of the 'wrong week to quit X' running gag, which will escalate to smoking, amphetamines, and glue-sniffing. Each entry is independently funny but the gag compounds beautifully across the film. Lloyd Bridges's framing — as though quitting drinking was the mistake, not the disaster — is perfect character comedy. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Kramer, privately: 'Shit! It's a goddamn waste of time. There's no way he can land it! You got to talk him down! Route him into Lake Michigan. At least avoid killing innocent people.'
jokes.setup: Kramer is supposed to be building Striker's confidence; he has just said 'Our one hope is to build this man up.'
jokes.punchline: The moment the radio is live he screams 'Shit! Goddamn waste of time! Route him into Lake Michigan!' — his private despair is the total opposite of his public encouragement.
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — Kramer's duty to encourage Striker versus his private conviction it's hopeless. 'Route him into Lake Michigan' is a great dark-comedy kicker: the 'backup plan' is to crash the plane somewhere with fewer innocent victims. The gap between his public and private voice is well-exploited.

jokes.text: Kramer tries to build Striker's confidence: 'Flying a plane is no different from riding a bicycle — it's just harder to put baseball cards in the spokes.'
jokes.setup: Kramer is supposed to give Striker a confidence-building analogy to make flying feel accessible.
jokes.punchline: His analogy degrades into a nonsensical comparison about baseball cards in bicycle spokes — a completely irrelevant detail delivered as though it's the key insight.
jokes.explanation: Superb absurdist construction. The setup ('riding a bicycle') is a real platitude; the punchline takes it in the most specific, irrelevant direction imaginable. 'Baseball cards in the spokes' is unexpected, concrete, and utterly useless as advice — which is the entire joke. High originality because the specificity of the image is genuinely surprising.

jokes.text: Elaine tells passengers: 'The other two pilots are fine. They're flying the plane, free to pursue a life of religious fulfilment.'
jokes.setup: Elaine is trying to reassure panicking passengers. She admits one crew member is 'slightly ill.'
jokes.punchline: She claims the other two pilots are 'fine' and 'flying the plane, free to pursue a life of religious fulfilment' — an absurd euphemism for the fact that they are incapacitated (or in this case, using ZAZ's running gag about the pilots being incapacitated and presumably doing something else).
jokes.explanation: Sharp ironic euphemism. 'Free to pursue a life of religious fulfilment' is a bizarrely specific and ornate way to say 'comatose from food poisoning.' The formal language makes the lie more absurd, and it callbacks nicely to the earlier pilot incapacitation setup.

jokes.text: Kramer aside: 'It's damn good he doesn't know I hate his guts.' / Rumack (or airport voice) immediately: 'It's damn good you don't know he hates your guts.'
jokes.setup: Kramer mutters privately that it's lucky Striker doesn't know he hates him.
jokes.punchline: The camera/audience is immediately told that Striker knows — delivered in the same register — revealing that the mutual hatred is known on both sides, undercutting Kramer's smugness.
jokes.explanation: Elegant parallel construction. The joke is built on the symmetry: Kramer thinks he has the upper hand in ignorance; the immediate cutaway/response reveals the secret is shared. The mirrored phrasing ('It's damn good he doesn't know' / 'It's damn good you don't know') is structurally immaculate. One of the reel's smarter jokes.

jokes.text: Jive-talking patient says something unintelligible. Elaine: 'I'm sorry. I don't understand.' An older woman steps in: 'Stewardess. I speak jive.' She translates: 'He said he's in great pain, and he wants to know if you can help him?'
jokes.setup: An ill passenger is speaking in jive slang that Elaine can't understand — a communication barrier during a crisis.
jokes.punchline: An elderly white woman casually announces 'I speak jive' and delivers a fluent, serious translation — the juxtaposition of her demographic against the fluency is the entire joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic gags. The surprise of the translator's identity — an apparently prim older woman — combined with her total confidence and the gravity of her delivery, is a textbook subversion of expectations. High impact because the visual of the character sells the joke even more than the line itself. Barbara Billingsley's casting makes it legendary.

jokes.text: 'What can you make out of this?' (handing over weather bulletin) / 'This? I can make a hat or a brooch or a pterodactyl...'
jokes.setup: McCroskey asks Johnny to analyze a weather bulletin: 'What can you make out of this?' — meaning 'What information can you derive from this?'
jokes.punchline: Johnny takes the question literally (what physical object can you make FROM this paper) and begins listing craft projects: 'a hat or a brooch or a pterodactyl...'
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best literalism jokes. The setup phrase 'what can you make of this' is completely idiomatic; Johnny's literal interpretation is perfect. The escalating list (hat → brooch → pterodactyl) is brilliantly structured — hat and brooch are plausible origami, then 'pterodactyl' detonates into pure absurdism. The ellipsis suggests he's continuing the list, which makes it funnier. Among the top 3 jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: McCroskey calls Captain Oveur's wife to report trouble, asks her to come to the airport. She says 'I'll be right down' — then we cut to her house, where she tells an unseen person: 'I've got to go to the airport. You can let yourself out the back door. There's juice in the refrigerator.'
jokes.setup: McCroskey calls Mrs. Oveur to relay a family emergency about her husband. She says she'll come right away — implying a devoted, concerned wife.
jokes.punchline: The cut to her house reveals she has a secret guest she's casually dismissing — implying infidelity. 'There's juice in the refrigerator' makes it mundanely domestic and funnier.
jokes.explanation: Efficient two-beat joke. The cut to her house and the casual 'there's juice in the refrigerator' is perfectly chosen — the hospitality detail makes the implied infidelity funnier than any explicit confirmation. Good misdirection through dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Striker in cockpit picks up the radio to concentrate. Radio voice: 'Echo!' — then a baseball announcer: 'Pinch hitting for Pedro Bourbone, Manny Mota.' [long pause] 'Manny... Mota.'
jokes.setup: Striker desperately picks up the radio for emergency instructions while trying to fly a doomed plane.
jokes.punchline: Instead of emergency communications, the radio gives him a stadium echo and a baseball game update — delivered with the reverent gravity of historic sports broadcasting.
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ random-channel absurdism. The 'Manny... Mota.' repeat with the reverent pause mimics the portentous drama of sports broadcasting — applied to a wholly irrelevant moment. The specificity of the name (Manny Mota was a real pinch-hitter) gives it authenticity that makes the absurdism land harder.

jokes.text: Patient in cabin: 'Jack, I'm so hot, I'm burning up.' / Jack: 'I'll turn on some air.' — then appears to open a window on a pressurized aircraft at altitude.
jokes.setup: A sick passenger complains of heat.
jokes.punchline: Jack casually responds by apparently opening a window on a commercial aircraft at 24,000 feet — which would be catastrophic — treating it as a mundane household solution.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag that works because of the matter-of-fact delivery. The horror of opening a plane window at altitude is treated with the casualness of opening a car window on a warm day. Impact depends heavily on the visual sell — 'What's going on? Close the window!' from other passengers confirms the gag.

jokes.text: McCroskey: 'Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit amphetamines.'
jokes.setup: Earlier McCroskey said he picked the wrong week to quit drinking. Now the crisis has deepened further.
jokes.punchline: The gag escalates: now it's amphetamines, not just alcohol — the self-medication options are getting harder and more illegal, reflecting the worsening crisis.
jokes.explanation: Second installment of the escalating 'wrong week to quit' gag, and it's funnier than the first precisely because of the escalation. Jumping from alcohol to amphetamines is a big leap that signals the gag will keep going, and the audience anticipates the next beat. Lloyd Bridges's performance — taking a swig or a pill with no commentary — would amplify this. One of the film's best running gags.

jokes.text: Press: 'Who's flying the plane?' / Airport rep: 'A passenger. He's an experienced air force pilot. No cause for alarm.' / Reporter: 'What kind of plane?' / Rep: 'It's a big, pretty white plane with red stripes, curtains and wheels. It looks like a big Tylenol.'
jokes.setup: Reporters ask the standard, serious question about the plane type for their news coverage.
jokes.punchline: The 'official' description of the aircraft is 'a big, pretty white plane with red stripes, curtains and wheels. It looks like a big Tylenol.' — the description of a child or someone who has never seen a plane.
jokes.explanation: Johnny's description is wonderfully naive and specific — 'curtains' and 'wheels' as notable features, then the kicker 'it looks like a big Tylenol.' That final simile is unexpected, oddly accurate, and delivered with complete seriousness. Very quotable. Good character specificity for Johnny's clueless-but-earnest persona.

jokes.text: Shana, they bought their tickets. They knew what they were getting into. I say, let them crash!
jokes.setup: McCroskey is told about the stricken airliner approaching Chicago, implying he should help
jokes.punchline: He dismisses the emergency with callous capitalist logic and concludes with 'let them crash' — the opposite of what a responsible air traffic controller should say
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it inverts the expected disaster-movie authority figure. The 'they bought their tickets' logic is absurdly airtight, and 'let them crash' as a conclusion is shockingly blunt. Good economy and dark subversive energy.

jokes.text: Would you like some whisky, ma'am? — Certainly not!
jokes.setup: Stewardess offers a passenger whisky in a crisis situation — a straight offer
jokes.punchline: The passenger refuses indignantly, but the visual joke (inferred from the film) is that the passenger is a nun or someone in an absurdly prim situation refusing comfort during a life-or-death emergency
jokes.explanation: A quick background gag — the prim refusal during a crisis is mildly amusing but not elaborated. Functional filler humor.

jokes.text: Surely, there's something you can do. — I'm doing everything I can... and stop calling me Shirley.
jokes.setup: In a tense crisis moment, someone pleads 'Surely, there's something you can do' — using 'surely' as a sincere adverb
jokes.punchline: Rumack hears 'Surely' as the name 'Shirley' and corrects the speaker mid-crisis with stone-faced literalism
jokes.explanation: One of the most famous jokes in cinematic comedy history. The setup is perfect — 'surely' used in a totally sincere, urgent context. The deadpan correction is completely unexpected. Leslie Nielsen's delivery is legendary. It's a pure literalism gag executed with flawless timing and economy. The joke earns its cultural touchstone status: it has become the defining example of the film's comedic mode. Genuinely a 9+ moment.

jokes.text: I'm scared. I've never been so scared... And besides, I'm 26 and I'm not married.
jokes.setup: Randy expresses existential fear about dying in the crash — a sincere emotional moment
jokes.punchline: She pivots from mortal terror to a completely trivial personal anxiety (not being married at 26), delivered as an equal or greater concern
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the emotional sincerity of the first two lines makes the trivial 'and besides, I'm 26 and not married' land as a sharp deflation. The 'and besides' construction is perfect, suggesting the marriage anxiety is somehow secondary when it's actually absurdly primary. Sharp economy.

jokes.text: To be honest, I've never been so scared, but at least I have a husband.
jokes.setup: Dr. Rumack asks how Elaine is bearing up, paralleling Randy's earlier confessional
jokes.punchline: Elaine mirrors Randy's exact phrasing about being scared but subverts it by citing having a husband as her comfort — which is ironic given Striker is the terrified, broken man about to attempt a crash landing
jokes.explanation: A tight callback that both mirrors Randy's structure and delivers its own irony: Elaine's comfort is 'having a husband' when that husband is the most terrified person on the plane. The parallel construction makes it land cleanly.

jokes.text: Repeating loop of war flashback dialogue: 'Stay in formation. Target's just ahead. You'll have to decide.' — playing on a stuck loop
jokes.setup: Striker's traumatic war flashback plays as a narrative device to explain his PTSD
jokes.punchline: The flashback loops and repeats identically, like a broken record — a visual/audio gag suggesting the memory is literally stuck on repeat, parodying disaster movie flashback clichés
jokes.explanation: A clever structural gag that parodies disaster-movie flashback conventions by literalizing the 'stuck in the past' idea. The repetition itself is the joke. Works better visually than on the page.

jokes.text: When Kramer hears about this, the shit's going to hit the fan.
jokes.setup: A controller warns that Kramer will be furious when he hears about the lost oil pressure — using the idiom 'the shit's going to hit the fan'
jokes.punchline: In the Airplane! universe, this is a literal visual setup — the film cuts to Kramer, and a fan with literal excrement hits him (inferred from the film's known visual gag)
jokes.explanation: Classic ZAZ literalism — takes a standard idiom and executes it visually. The setup is a straight use of the phrase, the payoff is the physical gag. Works because the deadpan delivery of the idiom earns the absurd visual payoff. One of the film's signature techniques.

jokes.text: It happened to Barbara Stanwyck.
jokes.setup: Controllers are arguing about Striker's psychological breakdown, with one saying 'it could happen to any pilot'
jokes.punchline: Someone deadpans 'It happened to Barbara Stanwyck' — a completely non sequitur celebrity reference that implies Barbara Stanwyck had a pilot breakdown, which is absurd
jokes.explanation: A perfectly timed non sequitur that works because of its complete specificity and confidence. The randomness of 'Barbara Stanwyck' as the example is the joke — delivered with total conviction as if it's a known fact. Pure ZAZ absurdism.

jokes.text: Nick, Pete, Jerry, there's a fire in the barn.
jokes.setup: In the middle of a tense cockpit crisis about whether Striker can land the plane, Rumack interjects with an urgent announcement
jokes.punchline: The announcement is a completely irrelevant rural emergency ('fire in the barn') addressed to random names, having nothing to do with the aviation crisis
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist non sequitur inserted into a tense scene. The specificity ('fire in the barn') and casual delivery in the middle of a plane emergency is funny. Slightly under-motivated but efficient.

jokes.text: Bad news. Fog's getting thicker. — And Leon's getting larger.
jokes.setup: Controller reports worsening fog conditions as a serious weather update during the emergency
jokes.punchline: Second controller non sequiturs with 'And Leon's getting larger' — delivered with equal gravity, as if Leon growing is of comparable meteorological concern
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The parallel grammatical structure ('Fog's getting thicker / Leon's getting larger') makes it land perfectly — the second line mimics the rhythm and gravity of the first, then delivers complete nonsense. 'Leon' is never explained, which makes it funnier. High quotability, deeply absurdist, and structurally flawless. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: The pilot's name was George Zip.
jokes.setup: Rumack delivers an earnest, moving war story about an inspirational pilot who spoke wise last words about perseverance
jokes.punchline: The pilot's name is revealed to be 'George Zip' — setting up the punchline that his famous last words were 'win one for the Zipper'
jokes.explanation: A masterfully constructed extended parody of the 'win one for the Gipper' speech. The name 'George Zip' is revealed with the same gravitas as a legend, and 'Zip' as a name is inherently funny while also setting up 'the Zipper.' The long build makes the payoff proportionally bigger. Well-earned 8+.

jokes.text: George Zip said that?
jokes.setup: Rumack has just delivered the name 'George Zip' with great reverence
jokes.punchline: Striker repeats it back as a question — not reacting to the absurdity of the name but treating it as a profound revelation, as if 'George Zip' is a legend he's heard of
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat is essential to the George Zip sequence. Striker's sincere repetition ('George Zip said that?') treats the absurd name as gospel — the deadpan plays perfectly off Rumack's straight delivery. Part of a longer comedic build.

jokes.text: Win just one for the Zipper.
jokes.setup: The George Zip speech has been building as a parody of the 'win one for the Gipper' Knute Rockne/Reagan speech
jokes.punchline: 'The Zipper' as the nickname for someone named Zip — a ridiculous but internally logical nickname that also sounds inherently undignified
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the extended George Zip setup. 'The Zipper' as a nickname is funny on its own and lands as a perfect parody punchline to the Gipper reference. The long setup earns this. The whole George Zip sequence is one of the film's best sustained gags.

jokes.text: I don't know where I'll be then, but I won't smell too good, that's for sure.
jokes.setup: The George Zip speech reaches its emotional peak — the dying pilot's final poetic words about the future
jokes.punchline: Instead of a noble final sentiment, the dying pilot's last prediction is that he'll smell bad — delivered with Rumack's total gravitas
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the George Zip speech is the best line in it. After the earnest buildup, the pivot to 'I won't smell too good, that's for sure' is brilliantly deflating — it's dark (he's predicting his own corpse's decomposition) but delivered as a simple practical observation. Leslie Nielsen's deadpan makes this legendary. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: I guess the foot's on the other hand now.
jokes.setup: Striker defiantly tells Chicago he's taking control and coming in despite orders, implying the tables have turned
jokes.punchline: He attempts the idiom 'the shoe's on the other foot' but mangles it into 'the foot's on the other hand' — a malapropism that reveals his broken confidence through linguistic failure
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed malapropism that's character-specific — Striker's psychological fragility manifests as scrambled idioms throughout the film. The mangled phrase works because it's delivered as if he's making a triumphant declaration. High character integration.

jokes.text: He's boss, head man, top dog, big cheese, head honcho... Captain, look at this. 'Passengers certain to die.' 'Airline negligent.' There's a sale at Penny's!
