jokes.setup: McCroskey lists increasingly redundant synonyms for 'in charge' (boss, head man, top dog, big cheese, head honcho) in a mounting series — then is interrupted by his assistant reading terrible newspaper headlines
jokes.punchline: After two devastating headlines ('Passengers certain to die,' 'Airline negligent'), the assistant reads 'There's a sale at Penny's!' with identical urgency and gravity
jokes.explanation: A two-part joke with both parts earning their laugh. The escalating synonyms (boss → head man → top dog → big cheese → head honcho) is funny on its own as absurd redundancy. Then the headlines sequence adds a perfect third-beat: two genuine emergencies capped by the trivial sale announcement delivered with equal gravity. Classic ZAZ bathos. High impact, well-structured.

jokes.text: Me John. Big tree.
jokes.setup: McCroskey assigns tower personnel by name: 'You, Neubauer, you, Macias'
jokes.punchline: Macias responds with 'Me John. Big tree.' — a Tarzan-esque non sequitur that makes no sense in context and is never explained
jokes.explanation: A quick background absurdist gag. The Tarzan reference is a bit dated and the joke is more random than earned, but the confidence and economy of delivery saves it. Filler-level but functional.

jokes.text: They're going to the tower. The tower! The tower! Rapunzel! Rapunzel!
jokes.setup: Someone announces matter-of-factly that the team is going to the tower
jokes.punchline: An unseen person in the background shouts 'The tower! The tower! Rapunzel! Rapunzel!' — a fairy-tale free-association triggered by the word 'tower'
jokes.explanation: A quick background gag that works on pure wordplay — 'tower' triggers 'Rapunzel.' The escalation from a matter-of-fact statement to a fairy tale shout is funny. Slight but efficient.

jokes.text: Captain McCroskey, this is Captain Roberts. Captain Kramer, this is Captain Colosimo. Captain Hinshaw, this is Captain Gantz. Captain Kramer, Captain Gantz. Captain Hinshaw, Captain Roberts.
jokes.setup: In a crisis, the tower is filling with captains and McCroskey begins introducing them to each other
jokes.punchline: The introductions escalate into a bewildering round-robin of captain names with no apparent purpose, taking time away from the actual emergency
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurd formality of endless introductions during a life-or-death crisis. The rhythm is funny but it goes slightly long. Works as background comic texture.

jokes.text: Get that finger out of your ear. You don't know where it's been.
jokes.setup: McCroskey is briskly assigning tasks to controllers in a crisis
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his emergency commands to reprimand a controller for picking his ear, delivering the classic parental phrase 'You don't know where it's been' as if it's equally urgent
jokes.explanation: Classic bathos — the mundane parental scolding inserted into urgent crisis management. The phrase 'you don't know where it's been' applied to your own finger is a nicely absurd take on a familiar expression. Good economy.

jokes.text: Your husband and the others are alive but unconscious. — Just like Gerald Ford.
jokes.setup: Rumack delivers the medical status of the sick passengers — 'alive but unconscious'
jokes.punchline: Someone deadpans 'Just like Gerald Ford' — equating the unconscious passengers with the supposedly mentally absent president
jokes.explanation: A quick political joke with perfect economy. The Gerald Ford 'unconscious/absent' gag is a topical joke that played well in 1980. The deadpan insertion is sharp. Slightly dated now but structurally clean.

jokes.text: Where did you get that dress? It's awful! And those shoes and that coat! Geez!
jokes.setup: Rumack has been delivering urgent medical updates about dying passengers
jokes.punchline: He suddenly turns to a woman and delivers a withering fashion critique with apparent sincerity, completely outside his role as a doctor in a crisis
jokes.explanation: A perfectly absurd character break — Rumack's gravitas makes this unexpected diversion into fashion criticism funnier. The specificity ('and those shoes and that coat!') commits to the bit. Works because Leslie Nielsen plays it straight.

jokes.text: Air Israel, please clear the runway.
jokes.setup: The tower is methodically clearing emergency vehicles and assigning runway positions
jokes.punchline: In the middle of assigning Air Force positions and ambulances, the controller casually asks 'Air Israel' to clear the runway — implying Air Israel is inexplicably parked there
jokes.explanation: A quick background joke — the random specificity of 'Air Israel' parked on the runway during an American emergency is quietly absurd. Delivered deadpan in a list, it works as a quick laugh.

jokes.text: WZAZ in Chicago, where disco lives forever.
jokes.setup: The cockpit is tuned in for emergency radio contact during landing approach; the life-jacket safety briefing has just been delivered
jokes.punchline: Instead of emergency communications, the radio outputs a cheesy disco station ID — 'WZAZ in Chicago, where disco lives forever' — in 1980 when disco was emphatically dead
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing — a station ID materializes in the middle of a safety briefing. 'Where disco lives forever' is a sharp meta-cultural joke in 1980 since disco had recently and famously died. The confidence of its intrusion is the joke.

jokes.text: Captain, maybe we ought to turn on the searchlights. — No. That's just what they'll be expecting us to do.
jokes.setup: During final approach in fog and darkness, a tower crewman suggests turning on searchlights to help the pilot land
jokes.punchline: McCroskey refuses with strategic military logic — 'that's just what they'll be expecting us to do' — as if landing the plane is an adversarial game against an enemy
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. McCroskey treats a straightforward safety suggestion as a tactical blunder, applying war-movie logic to a civilian emergency landing. 'That's just what they'll be expecting us to do' — implying a 'they' that doesn't exist — is a perfect character joke and a great parody of military movie tropes. Very quotable, well-structured, earns its 8+.

jokes.text: I want to tell you both good luck. We're all counting on you.
jokes.setup: Rumack appears at a critical moment and delivers an encouraging sendoff
jokes.punchline: This is the same line delivered identically multiple times throughout the reel (79:59, 80:14) — the repetition itself becomes the joke, with Rumack reappearing to deliver it like a broken record
jokes.explanation: A running gag that becomes funnier each repetition. Rumack keeps materializing to deliver the identical line with identical gravity, as if each appearance is a fresh intervention. The joke is in the structure: it appears three times in this reel alone, and the third appearance (during the chaotic landing) is the funniest because of the accumulated repetition. Scores the running gag, not just the first instance.

jokes.text: Sure is quiet out there. — Yeah, too quiet.
jokes.setup: Two controllers are watching the final approach; this is a parody of a Western/thriller cliché
jokes.punchline: 'Too quiet' — a direct lift of the Western movie cliché, deployed deadpan in an airport tower during a crisis, implying unseen Apache warriors rather than fog
jokes.explanation: A reliable genre-parody gag — the Western 'too quiet' cliché is a known quantity. It works here because of perfect deadpan delivery and the incongruity of an airport tower, but it's a borrowed joke structure rather than an original one.

jokes.text: Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit sniffing glue.
jokes.setup: Throughout the film (callbacks to earlier reels), characters have said 'I picked the wrong week to quit [substance],' escalating from cigarettes to amphetamines
jokes.punchline: The final entry in the escalating list is 'sniffing glue' — the most ridiculous and juvenile substance yet, delivered with identical world-weary resignation
jokes.explanation: The climax of one of the film's best running gags. Each escalation is funnier than the last, and 'sniffing glue' as the final entry is perfect — it's juvenile, oddly specific, and completely undermines Rumack's authoritative doctor persona. The structure of the running gag (identical setup, escalating substance) is textbook comedy escalation. Very high quotability. Earns the 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Striker, you're coming in too fast. — I know, I know! — He knows, he knows!
jokes.setup: Tower warns Striker about his speed; Striker confirms he knows
jokes.punchline: Elaine echoes Striker's reply to the tower ('He knows, he knows!') as if relaying information the tower didn't already receive from Striker himself, adding a layer of panicked redundancy
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation joke — the three-beat rhythm (warning / acknowledgment / redundant echo) is clean and efficient. Elaine's anxious relay is a nice character beat. Funny in the moment.

jokes.text: 900 up to 1,300 feet. What an asshole.
jokes.setup: A controller is reading out Striker's wildly erratic altitude in a tense professional voice
jokes.punchline: He appends 'What an asshole' in the same professional tone, as if it's a standard technical observation about the pilot's performance
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan. The professional aviation readout voice delivering 'What an asshole' as if it's a formal evaluation is a great tonal subversion. The economy is flawless — the entire joke is four words appended to a technical readout. High quotability and impact.

jokes.text: Just kidding!
jokes.setup: In the middle of frantic, urgent landing instructions ('Get ready to flare it out! He's all over the place...'), a voice suddenly says 'Just kidding!'
jokes.punchline: In the most dangerous moment of the film, someone in the tower breaks the fourth wall of the disaster movie genre to announce they were joking — then immediately continues with real instructions
jokes.explanation: A quick but effective meta-gag — breaking the tension of the landing sequence with an inexplicable 'just kidding' is jarring and funny. The casualness of it undercuts the disaster-movie urgency perfectly.

jokes.text: Gate 13... Gate 14. Gate 15... [plane crashing through terminals] Gate 23, 24, 25...
jokes.setup: The plane has landed but is careening out of control through the airport; the PA system calmly announces gates
jokes.punchline: As the plane destroys gate after gate, the announcer's calm gate-change announcement keeps pace with the destruction, the numbers climbing as the plane crashes through each one
jokes.explanation: A great sustained visual/audio gag. The PA announcer's calm tone against the destruction escalates perfectly — the incremental gate numbers become a comedic odometer of chaos. Great structure and visual commitment.

jokes.text: Auntie Em! Toto! It's a twister!
jokes.setup: The plane is spinning/skidding wildly through the airport in what looks like a tornado of chaos
jokes.punchline: A passenger screams a Wizard of Oz reference — 'Auntie Em! Toto! It's a twister!' — as if the spinning airport is the tornado sequence from the film
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/verbal gag — the Wizard of Oz reference is triggered by the spinning chaos. Familiar pop-culture joke, slightly cheap but efficiently deployed. Works in context.

jokes.text: I want to tell you both good luck. We're all counting on you. [third repetition during post-landing chaos]
jokes.setup: Rumack reappears after the chaotic landing to deliver his now-familiar line
jokes.punchline: The third identical repetition of the line, now completely disconnected from any logical context (the plane has already landed), becomes the funniest iteration by virtue of pure repetition and inapplicability
jokes.explanation: The third iteration of the running gag is structurally the funniest — it fires after the landing is already complete, making Rumack's encouragement hilariously pointless. The rule of three makes this land bigger than the previous two. High rewatch bonus because on rewatch you anticipate and enjoy the third appearance.

jokes.text: Ted, that was probably the lousiest landing in the history of this airport. But some of us, particularly me, would like to buy you a drink and shake your hand.
jokes.setup: Striker has just completed the most disastrous landing in cinematic history, destroying multiple gates
jokes.punchline: Kramer opens with an honest, devastating assessment ('the lousiest landing in the history of this airport') and then pivots to sincere congratulations with 'particularly me' — an oddly self-centered qualification
jokes.explanation: A satisfying payoff moment. Kramer's brutal-then-warm assessment works as character comedy — the 'lousiest landing' opening subverts the expected congratulatory speech, and 'particularly me' adds an oddly specific self-insertion that's funny.

jokes.text: Have a nice day. OK. Have a nice day and thank you for flying TransAmerican.
jokes.setup: Passengers are evacuating after the plane has crashed through most of the airport and they nearly died
jokes.punchline: Randy delivers the standard airline departure pleasantries ('Have a nice day. Thank you for flying TransAmerican') as if this were a normal flight, completely ignoring the catastrophe
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to airline normalcy — after an extraordinary disaster, the mundane professionalism of 'have a nice day' is a perfect tonal contrast. Character-specific: Randy has been cheerfully oblivious throughout.

jokes.text: Have a nice day. OK. Have a nice day and thank you for flying TransAmerican.
jokes.setup: Passengers have just survived a near-fatal crash landing after hours of terror
jokes.punchline: Randy gives the standard flight-attendant farewell as if this were a routine departure — 'have a nice day and thank you for flying TransAmerican'
jokes.explanation: Irony of returning to mundane professional courtesy after a disaster. The cheerful routine farewell after near-death lands as a satisfying punctuation mark. Character-appropriate for Randy.

jokes.text: Loneliness, that's the bottom line. I was never happy as a child. Christmas, what does that mean to you? Mine was living hell. Do you know what it's like to fall in the mud and get kicked in the head by an iron boot? Of course not. It never happens. Sorry. That's a dumb question. Skip that.
jokes.setup: After the heroic landing and congratulations, Striker turns to debrief or speak — the audience expects a heroic or emotional resolution
jokes.punchline: Striker launches into a completely unrelated, self-pitying monologue about childhood loneliness, culminating in the absurd 'kicked in the head by an iron boot' — then self-corrects ('That's a dumb question. Skip that'), puncturing his own pathos
jokes.explanation: A great character comedy moment — Striker's post-crisis unraveling into self-pity is funny because it's so inappropriate and specific. 'Kicked in the head by an iron boot? Of course not. It never happens. Sorry. That's a dumb question.' is a perfect self-aware escalation and self-correction. The specificity of 'iron boot' and the apologetic correction ('skip that') make this a standout. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Municipal bonds, Ted. Talking double 'A' rating. Best investment in America.
jokes.setup: After the heroic landing, we expect some kind of emotional or dramatic resolution; a passenger approaches Striker
jokes.punchline: The passenger — who has been hounding Striker for investment advice throughout the film — ignores the life-or-death event entirely and pitches municipal bonds, capping the film's running joke
jokes.explanation: A perfect final-act callback. After surviving a near-death crash, the most urgent thing on this passenger's mind is municipal bonds. The specificity ('double A rating') and the complete indifference to the near-tragedy make this a satisfying comedic button to the film. High economy and character specificity earn the 8+.

jokes.text: Well, I'll give him another 20 minutes, but that's it.
jokes.setup: The film's final joke — referencing the inflatable autopilot 'Otto' who has been 'flying' the plane (or some unresolved waiting situation)
jokes.punchline: After the entire film, someone is still casually waiting with a '20 more minutes' deadline, as if the emergency that just concluded was merely an inconvenience delaying something
jokes.explanation: A quiet final button joke. The casual 'give him another 20 minutes' implies someone (Otto the inflatable autopilot, or a waiting character) is still in a holding pattern. The understatement after the epic chaos is a satisfying final note.
